citation.title: On the Foundations of the Design-Based Approach

standing_assumptions:
The work is a main article of 16 pages (Political Analysis (2026), 0, 1–16, doi:10.1017/pan.2026.10045; printed page = PDF page) and a publisher's Supplementary Appendix of 10 pages (publisher-supplement.pdf; printed page = PDF page, the first page unnumbered). The main text states no numbered theorem: its formal content is the setup of Section 3, Equations (1)–(8), Conditions 4.1, 5.1 and 5.2 and the worked Tables 1–5. The supplement carries its own Equations (1)–(11), Conditions 1.1–1.3 and Proposition 1; they are cited below as ‘supplement Equation (k)’ and so on. Everything quoted was read from the page images.
(S1) Probability space. p. 3, Section 3: “we formalize the design in terms of a probability triple $(\Omega,S,P)$, where the sample space, $\Omega$, consists of all conceivable experimental (or sampling) interventions and each realized intervention, $\omega$, refers to the vector of treatment (or sampling) assignments to all $N$ observations. The event space is the power set of the sample space, $S=\mathcal P(\Omega)$ and we assume that our probability measure satisfies $\Pr[A]=\sum_{\omega\in A}p(\omega),\ \forall A\in S$, where $p:\Omega\to[0,1]$, with $p(\omega)$ characterizing the probability of the assignment of an intervention.”
(S2) Design and design space. p. 3, Section 3.1: “We define the design space $\mathcal Z=\mathbf Z(\Omega)$, where $\mathbf Z$ is a bijective random vector $\mathbf Z:\Omega\to\mathbb R^N$. The design is defined as the joint p.m.f. of $\mathbf Z$, $f:\mathbb R^N\to[0,1]$. We may define all objects with respect to the design vector $\mathbf Z$, removing all notational dependence on $\omega$. We assume that the design is determined by the researcher”. ‘Bijective’ is read as injective, that is, a bijection of $\Omega$ onto $\mathcal Z$ (finding P061-N003, a clarity note); the inverse in Equation (1) is applied only on $\mathcal Z$. $\mathcal Z$ is the set of feasible interventions and may be strictly larger than the support of the design (p. 8: “$\mathcal Z$ may include assignments outside the design”).
(S3) Population and raw potential outcomes. p. 4, Section 3.2: “This finite population is indexed by $i=1,\ldots,N$, where indexing is fixed.” “We represent the outcomes of interest associated with these units with a real-valued random vector, $\mathbf Y$. The random vector $\mathbf Y$ characterizes the raw potential outcomes, which can be represented for each individual $i$ as $$y_i(\mathbf z)=Y_i(\mathbf Z^{-1}(\mathbf z)),\ \forall i\in 1,\ldots,N,\ \mathbf z\in\mathcal Z.\qquad(1)$$ The raw potential outcome $y_i(\mathbf z)$ for individual $i$ is what we observe if we perform intervention $\mathbf z$ and measure unit $i$’s outcome. There are a total of $N\times|\mathcal Z|$ raw potential outcomes in the causal setting.” The observed outcome is $Y_i=y_i(\mathbf Z)$ (supplement p. 2: “we use the fact that $Y_i=y_i(\mathbf Z)$, from the definition of raw potential outcomes given in Section 3”).
(S4) Exposure mapping. p. 4, Section 3.3: “Formally, our exposure mapping for individual $i$ is a function $g_i:\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$.” “Given that we have knowledge of the support of the design vector, $\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z)$, we can define a function $g_i|_{\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z)}:\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z)\to\mathbb R$. We denote the $N$-length random exposure vector $$\mathbf D=(g_1(\mathbf Z),g_2(\mathbf Z),\ldots,g_N(\mathbf Z)).\qquad(2)$$” The mappings used in the paper's examples: the ‘individualistic’ mapping (p. 5) $g_i(\mathbf z)=\begin{cases}1&:z_i=1\\0&:\text{otherwise}\end{cases},\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\},\mathbf z\in\{0,1\}^N$ (written $g_i(\mathbf z)=z_i$ on p. 8); the network mapping (p. 5) $$g_i(\mathbf z)=\begin{cases}0\ (\text{Control})&:\text{ if }z_i=0\text{ and }\theta_i\mathbf z=0,\\1\ (\text{Isolated Direct})&:\text{ if }z_i=1\text{ and }\theta_i\mathbf z=0,\\2\ (\text{Indirect})&:\text{ if }z_i=0\text{ and }\theta_i\mathbf z>0,\\3\ (\text{Direct \& Indirect})&:\text{ if }z_i=1\text{ and }\theta_i\mathbf z>0,\end{cases}\quad\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\},\ \mathbf z\in\{0,1\}^N,\qquad(3)$$ “where $\theta_i$ is the $i$th row of the network adjacency matrix”; and the coarsened mapping of Section 6.2 (p. 11) $g_i(\mathbf z)=\begin{cases}1&:z_i>0\\0&:\text{otherwise}\end{cases},\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\},\mathbf z\in\{0,1,2\}^N$.
(S5) Exposure probability, positivity, EPO. p. 6, Section 4.1: “we denote the marginal probability that unit $i$ enters exposure $d$ under the design distribution of $\mathbf Z$ as $$\pi_i(d)=\Big(\sum_{\mathbf z\in\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z):g_i(\mathbf z)=d}\Pr[\mathbf Z=\mathbf z]\Big)=\Pr[D_i=d].\qquad(4)$$” “Condition 4.1 (Individual positivity). An exposure $d$ satisfies individual positivity if there exists a $c$ such that $0<c\le\pi_i(d)\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$.” “Given that relevant individual positivity assumptions hold, the EPO for unit $i$ under exposure $d$ is defined as $$\overline y_i(d)=\frac{\sum_{\mathbf z\in\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z):g_i(\mathbf z)=d}y_i(\mathbf z)\Pr[\mathbf Z=\mathbf z]}{\sum_{\mathbf z\in\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z):g_i(\mathbf z)=d}\Pr[\mathbf Z=\mathbf z]}=\mathrm E[y_i(\mathbf Z)|g_i(\mathbf Z)=d]=\mathrm E[y_i(\mathbf Z)|D_i=d].\qquad(5)$$” “To avoid notational overload, these definitions implicitly hold fixed the exposure mapping $g$ and design $\mathbf Z$.” Where two designs are compared the paper writes $\tau_{\mathbf Z}$, $\tau_{\mathbf Z'}$ (Tables 4 and 5, Section 6.3).
(S6) AEPO, EED, AEED. p. 7: “Under individual positivity (Condition 4.1) for exposure $d$ and all individuals $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$, we average the EPOs over the units in the population to define the AEPO as $$\overline y(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\overline y_i(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm E[y_i(\mathbf Z)|D_i=d].\qquad(6)$$” “For an individual observation $i$, assuming that Condition 4.1 holds for exposures $d$ and $d'$ for all individuals $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$, we can define the EED between $d$ and $d'$ as $$\tau_i(d,d')=\overline y_i(d)-\overline y_i(d').\qquad(7)$$” “The AEED between $d$ and $d'$ is $$\tau(d,d')=\overline y(d)-\overline y(d')=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\tau_i(d,d').\qquad(8)$$” Footnote 8 (p. 7): “We compare this to the assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effect defined in Sävje, Aronow, and Hudgens (2021): $\tau_i^{AC}(d,d',\mathbf z_{-i})=y_i(d;\mathbf z_{-i})-y_i(d';\mathbf z_{-i})$. In the assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effect, we hold constant treatments assigned to all other individuals at $\mathbf z_{-i}$.”
(S7) Stability conditions. p. 8, Section 5.1: “Condition 5.1 (NURVA). $$g_i(\mathbf z)=g_i(\mathbf z')\implies y_i(\mathbf z)=y_i(\mathbf z')=\overline y_i(g_i(\mathbf z)),\ \forall\mathbf z,\mathbf z'\in\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z).$$” “Condition 5.2 (SUTVA). $$g_i(\mathbf z)=g_i(\mathbf z')\implies y_i(\mathbf z)=y_i(\mathbf z')=\overline y_i(g_i(\mathbf z)),\ \forall\mathbf z,\mathbf z'\in\mathcal Z.$$”
(S8) Estimator. Supplement p. 1: “Throughout, we will require the individual positivity, Condition 4.1, referenced in Section 4.” “We use the Horvitz-Thompson inverse probability weighted estimator (Horvitz and Thompson 1952), as defined in Equation 1, $$\hat{\overline y}(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Y_i\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{\pi_i(d)}.\qquad(1)$$” Supplement p. 4: “For the AEED, define $\hat\tau(d,d')=\hat{\overline y}(d)-\hat{\overline y}(d')$ and $\pi_{ij}(d,d')=\Pr[D_i=d,D_j=d']$.” Supplement p. 3: “Let the joint exposure probability, $\pi_{ij}(d)=\Pr[D_i=D_j=d]$.”
(S9) Asymptotic regime. Supplement p. 5: “We define a sequence of finite populations $U_{(N)}$ indexed by population size $N$. Associated with each finite population $U_{(N)}$ is a known random design vector $\mathbf Z_{(N)}$, a feasible intervention set $\mathcal Z_{(N)}$, $N$ exposure mappings $g_{i,(N)}:\mathcal Z_{(N)}\to\mathbb R$, and $N\times|\mathcal Z_{(N)}|$ raw potential outcomes. Assume that the range of $g_{i,(N)}|\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z_{(N)})$ contains $d$, for all $i,N$. The observed data is $(\mathbf Z_{(N)},\mathbf Y_{(N)})$. We let $N$ tend to infinity.” Note 2 (supplement p. 10): “In the asymptotic regime we could also index observations of, e.g., $y_i$ and $\pi_i(d)$ by $(N)$ but we leave this indexing implicit below.”
(S10) What the paper does not state, and how it is read here. (a) $\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z)$ is not defined; it is read as $\{\mathbf z\in\mathcal Z:\Pr[\mathbf Z=\mathbf z]>0\}$. (b) ‘Finite population’ restricts $N$, not the number of assignments: by (S1) the support is countable, and nothing makes it finite. Every design in the paper's examples and tables has finite support; the general setup admits a countably infinite support with unbounded outcomes (finding P061-CAND-001). (c) No integrability condition is stated anywhere. (d) Conditions 5.1 and 5.2 print no quantifier over $i$; they are read as holding for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Their last equality, $=\overline y_i(g_i(\mathbf z))$, involves an EPO that Equation (5) defines only when $\pi_i(g_i(\mathbf z))>0$: under Condition 5.1 this is automatic and the equality follows from the first one; under Condition 5.2 it is read as holding wherever the EPO is defined (finding P061-CAND-003, a clarity note, whose repair deletes that equality from Condition 5.2). (e) The notation $y_i(d;\mathbf z_{-i})$ of footnote 8 is not defined further; it is read as the raw potential outcome at the assignment vector whose $i$th coordinate is $d$ and whose other coordinates are $\mathbf z_{-i}$, which presupposes that the labels $d,d'$ are assignment coordinates and that the hybrid vector lies in $\mathcal Z$. (f) All probabilities, expectations, variances and covariances are over the design distribution of $\mathbf Z$, with the raw potential outcomes fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 8 (Conclusion), second paragraph, the ‘average direct effect’ sentence: counterexample with coarsened treatment versions
canonical_claim.location: p. 14 (PDF p. 14); the ingredients of the example are those of Section 6.2, pp. 11–12 (PDF pp. 11–12)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Raw potential outcomes on $\mathcal Z$: Equation (1), p. 4 (S3). Exposure vector $\mathbf D$: Equation (2), p. 4 (S4). The mapping $g_i(\mathbf z)=\mathbb 1\{z_i>0\}$ on $\{0,1,2\}^N$: Section 6.2, p. 11 (S4). $\pi_i(d)$, Condition 4.1 and the EPO $\overline y_i(d)$: Equations (4)–(5), p. 6 (S5). EED and AEED: Equations (7)–(8), p. 7 (S6). The notation $y_i(d;\mathbf z_{-i})$: footnote 8, p. 7 (S6), read as in (S10)(e); $y_i(1;\mathbf D_{-i})$ is the raw potential outcome at the vector whose $i$th coordinate is 1 and whose other coordinates are the other units' exposures, which here lies in $\{0,1\}^N\subseteq\mathcal Z$. ‘No interference’ in the sense of p. 12: “$y_i(\mathbf z)=y_i(\mathbf z')$ if $z_i=z_i'$”. $\hat{\overline y}(d)$ and $\hat\tau(d,d')$: supplement Equation (1), p. 1, and the definition before supplement Equation (9), p. 4 (S8). The printed sentence: P061-T22.
canonical_claim.note: P061-CAND-007 is rated an error, Moderate (ratings.json); Sol's verdict is confirmed in part, upheld on re-run. This is Section 3 of the validator's derivation (part B of check_exact.py, which enumerates $N=1,2,4,6$ in exact rational arithmetic; the algebra covers every $N$). What it refutes: the printed comparison when the AEED is formed with a coarsened exposure mapping, which the paper's framework allows and Section 6.2 itself uses; a design with independent exposures, bounded outcomes and no between-unit interference has a gap of $\tfrac12$ at every $N$. What it does not refute: the comparison restricted to assignment-coordinate exposures (P061-T3(i)), a version-mixing stochastic intervention (an equal mixture of versions 1 and 2 gives $\tfrac32$), or any theorem of Sävje (2024), which is not staged. Part (d) covers both the printed argument $\mathbf D_{-i}$ and the repaired argument $\mathbf Z_{-i}$: replacing $\mathbf D$ by $\mathbf Z$ alone does not remove the gap. The values in (b)–(e) and (g) were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic for $N=1,2,3$ when this list was fixed. The statement is exact at every finite $N$, so it is not marked asymptotic.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 8 (Conclusion), second paragraph, the ‘average direct effect’ sentence: the displayed expression is undefined under the paper's own network mapping, Equation (3)
canonical_claim.location: p. 14 (PDF p. 14); the mapping is Equation (3), p. 5 (PDF p. 5)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The network exposure mapping: Equation (3), p. 5 (S4), with $\theta_i$ the $i$th row of the network adjacency matrix. Raw potential outcomes with domain $\mathcal Z$: Equation (1), p. 4 (S3). $\mathbf D$: Equation (2), p. 4 (S4). $\pi_i(d)$, Condition 4.1, EPO: Equations (4)–(5), p. 6 (S5). AEED: Equation (8), p. 7 (S6). Conditions 5.1 and 5.2: p. 8 (S7), read as in (S10)(d). The notation $y_i(d;\cdot)$: footnote 8, p. 7, read as in (S10)(e). $g(\mathcal Z)$ denotes the image of $\mathcal Z$ under $\mathbf z\mapsto(g_1(\mathbf z),g_2(\mathbf z))$ (not the paper's notation). The printed sentence: P061-T22.
canonical_claim.note: Section 2 of the validator's derivation (part A of check_exact.py). It is a counterexample to well-definedness, not to an equality: the printed formula gives exposure labels to a function whose domain is the assignment space. The failure is not a positivity failure and is not removed by outcome stability, since SUTVA holds in the example. A Lean statement can certify (a)–(d) as finite facts about membership in $g(\mathcal Z)$ and in $\mathcal Z$; it cannot ‘prove undefinedness’ of an informal expression, so the faithful form is: there is no draw on which both arguments lie in the relevant domain (reading (c)), and the set of draws on which both lie in $\mathcal Z$ has probability $\tfrac12$ (reading (d)). Sol notes that undefinedness is not universal across non-identity mappings: for some mappings the substituted labels are compatible raw assignments. The image, the two counts (0 of 4 draws; 2 of 4 draws) and the values in (b) were recomputed when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 8 (Conclusion), second paragraph, the ‘average direct effect’ sentence: corrected comparison of the AEED with the average direct effect
canonical_claim.location: p. 14 (PDF p. 14); the corrected notation follows footnote 8, p. 7 (PDF p. 7)
canonical_claim.statement:
Corrected form of the comparison (Sol's smallest repair and the validator's verified replacement). In the setting of Section 3, with the targeted first-moment condition of P061-T8 for the exposures $d$ and $d'$ (automatic when $\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z)$ is finite):
(i) Assignment-coordinate exposures. Let $g_i(\mathbf z)=z_i$ for every $i$ (so $\mathbf D=\mathbf Z$), let $\pi_i(d)>0$ and $\pi_i(d')>0$ for every $i$, and let $Z_i$ be independent of $\mathbf Z_{-i}$ for every $i$. Then for every $i$ and every $\mathbf w$ with $\Pr[\mathbf Z_{-i}=\mathbf w]>0$ the hybrid assignments $(d;\mathbf w)$ and $(d';\mathbf w)$ have positive probability, hence lie in $\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z)\subseteq\mathcal Z$; $\overline y_i(d)=\mathrm E[y_i(d;\mathbf Z_{-i})]$ and $\overline y_i(d')=\mathrm E[y_i(d';\mathbf Z_{-i})]$; and therefore $$\tau(d,d')=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm E\big[y_i(d;\mathbf Z_{-i})-y_i(d';\mathbf Z_{-i})\big]$$ exactly, at every $N$, with no SUTVA, NURVA or no-interference assumption.
(ii) General exposures with a consistent exposure-level schedule. For a general exposure mapping, let $D_i$ be independent of $\mathbf D_{-i}$ for every $i$, let $\pi_i(d)>0$ and $\pi_i(d')>0$ for every $i$, and suppose that for every $i$ there is a function $H_i$, defined at every exposure vector $(e;\mathbf r)$ with $e\in\{d,d'\}$ and $\Pr[\mathbf D_{-i}=\mathbf r]>0$, such that $y_i(\mathbf z)=H_i(g_1(\mathbf z),\ldots,g_N(\mathbf z))$ for every $\mathbf z\in\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z)$ with $g_i(\mathbf z)\in\{d,d'\}$. Then $\mathrm E[Y_i\mid D_i=e]=\mathrm E[H_i(e;\mathbf D_{-i})]$ for $e\in\{d,d'\}$, and $$\tau(d,d')=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm E\big[H_i(d;\mathbf D_{-i})-H_i(d';\mathbf D_{-i})\big].$$
Neither part asserts an equivalence of inference under dependent assignments: an extension to dependent designs requires additional explicit conditions (P061-T5).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $y_i(d;\mathbf z_{-i})$: footnote 8, p. 7 (S6), read as in (S10)(e); $(d;\mathbf w)$ is the assignment vector with $i$th coordinate $d$ and other coordinates $\mathbf w$. $\mathbf Z_{-i}$, $\mathbf D_{-i}$: the vectors $\mathbf Z$, $\mathbf D$ without their $i$th coordinate (the paper uses $\mathbf z_{-i}$ in footnote 8 and $\mathbf D_{-i}$ on p. 14 without further definition). $\pi_i(d)$ and $\overline y_i(d)$: Equations (4)–(5), p. 6 (S5). $\tau(d,d')$: Equation (8), p. 7 (S6). Independence of $Z_i$ and $\mathbf Z_{-i}$ (of $D_i$ and $\mathbf D_{-i}$) is under the design distribution. Targeted first-moment condition: $\sum_{\mathbf z\in\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z):g_i(\mathbf z)=e}|y_i(\mathbf z)|\Pr[\mathbf Z=\mathbf z]<\infty$ for every $i$ and $e\in\{d,d'\}$ (P061-T8); under the independence assumed in (i) and (ii) it is equivalent to integrability of $y_i(e;\mathbf Z_{-i})$, respectively of $H_i(e;\mathbf D_{-i})$. The schedule $H_i$ of (ii) is not an object of the paper; it is the validator's formulation of ‘a specified consistent response schedule on exposure vectors’.
canonical_claim.note: Sections 4 and 5 of the validator's derivation; (i) is its ‘completely verified replacement’ and (ii) is the prior correction's alternative, which the validator found correct with one change (the AEED's exposures must be aligned with the assignment coordinates in the first alternative). The repair costs a weaker conclusion: the closing comparison no longer applies to arbitrary exposure mappings under locality alone. (ii) adds a substantive structural assumption, the existence of $H_i$, which the paper's own hidden-version example violates (P061-T1(f)); under exposure independence and positivity every relevant hybrid exposure vector has positive joint probability, so consistency on the image of the support suffices and no off-support extension of $H_i$ is needed. The validator's exact checks: part C (binary assignments with independent probabilities $\tfrac13,\tfrac12,\tfrac23$ and $y_i(\mathbf z)=z_i+2z_{i+1}+3z_iz_{i+1}$ with cyclic subscripts: both sides equal $\tfrac52$, recomputed when this list was fixed) and part D (both sides equal 6). The hypothesis on first moments is not in Sol's wording for finite designs; it is added because every hypothesis must be explicit and the setup allows infinite support (P061-CAND-001). No result elsewhere in the paper uses the sentence.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 8 (Conclusion), second paragraph, the claim that inference on AEEDs is asymptotically equivalent to inference on the average direct effect under local dependence and interference: counterexample to the transfer of inference
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\tau(1,0)$: Equation (8), p. 7 (S6), with $\overline y_i(d)$ from Equation (5), p. 6 (S5). $y_i(d;\mathbf Z_{-i})$: footnote 8, p. 7, read as in (S10)(e); here every hybrid assignment lies in $\mathcal Z=\{0,1\}^N$. $\hat{\overline y}(d)$ and $\hat\tau(d,d')$: supplement Equation (1), p. 1, and p. 4 (S8); with exposure probabilities $\tfrac12$, $\hat\tau=\frac2N\sum_{i=1}^N(2D_i-1)Y_i$. The ‘partner’ of a unit is the other member of its pair. Maximum degree: in the graph on the $N$ units that joins two units whose assignments are dependent (respectively, joins $i$ to $j$ when $y_i$ depends on $z_j$); these graphs are not objects of the paper, which speaks only of dependence and interference being ‘sufficiently local’. The printed sentence: P061-T22.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: All of (a)–(f) are exact statements for each fixed $m\ge2$; the limits are read off them. The identities the validator's derivation rests on (Section 3 of derivation.md, equations (2)–(12)): (L1) $\Pr[D_j=1\mid D_i=1]=\frac{1+\rho}{2}$ and $\Pr[D_j=1\mid D_i=0]=\frac{1-\rho}{2}$ for partners $i,j$; (L2) $\hat\tau=\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^KB_k$, where the contribution of a pair with assignment $(x,y)$ is $B=2\{(2x-1)(1+ay)+(2y-1)(1+ax)\}$, taking the values $-4,\,-2a,\,-2a,\,4(1+a)$ at $(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)$; (L3) $\mathrm E[B]=2a\rho$, $\mathrm E[B^2]=8(1+\rho)(1+a)+(6+2\rho)a^2$, $\mathrm{Var}(B)=V_m$; (L4) by independence across pairs, $\mathrm{Var}[\hat\tau]=KV_m/N^2=V_m/(4m^8)$; (L5) $8\le V_m\le\tfrac{79}{4}<20$ for $m\ge2$; (L6) Chebyshev's inequality: $\Pr[|\hat\tau-T_N|\ge5s_N]\le\tfrac1{25}$, and for $m\ge5$, $5s_N\le\delta_N/2$, so $A_N=0\in C_m$ implies $|\hat\tau-T_N|\ge\delta_N/2$, an event of probability at most $4s_N^2/\delta_N^2$.
canonical_claim.note: P061-N009 is rated an error, Moderate (ratings.json). Sol's verdict was undetermined after validation (upheld on re-run) and became confirmed in part after the external check (runs/P061/settle/settled.json), which read Sävje (2024) as arXiv 2103.06471v2 with its supplement and Sävje, Aronow and Hudgens (2021) as arXiv 1711.06399v4: the cited central limit theorem stays centred on the AEED and states no transfer result, and this design meets its local conditions as read there (dependency neighbourhoods of size at most 2, bounded outcomes, exposure probabilities $\tfrac12$, variance of order $N^{-1}$). What the example refutes: that bounded-degree locality of dependence and interference, even together with a vanishing difference between the two targets, suffices for transferring first-order inference. What it does not refute: every possible meaning of the paper's undefined qualifier ‘sufficiently local’; stronger rate conditions make the claim true (P061-T5), which is why Sol's truth fields for the printed sentence are null. NURVA fails in the example (the outcome varies within an own-assignment exposure), so it does not contradict the supplement's results that require NURVA. Part (f) uses only Chebyshev's inequality and the exact standard error; the validator adds that the Lindeberg condition holds, so normal intervals fail as well, which is not part of this target. The rows $m=2,3,5,10$ of the validator's table ($T_N$, $A_N$, $V_m$, $\mathrm{Var}[\hat\tau]$, $\delta_N^2/s_N^2$) and a full enumeration at $K=2$, $m=2$ were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic when this list was fixed. The construction is for the populations $N=2m^8$, a subsequence of population sizes.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 8 (Conclusion), second paragraph, the claim that inference on AEEDs is asymptotically equivalent to inference on the average direct effect: corrected statement with the rate condition
canonical_claim.statement:
Corrected form of the claim (Sol's smallest repair), for individualistic assignment mappings, $g_i(\mathbf z)=z_i$ and $\mathbf D=\mathbf Z$ (the restriction required by P061-CAND-007, see P061-T3). Along the sequence of finite populations of the supplement (p. 5), let $T_N=\tau(d,d')$ be the AEED and $A_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm E[y_i(d;\mathbf Z_{-i})-y_i(d';\mathbf Z_{-i})]$ the average direct effect, the hybrid assignments $(d;\mathbf Z_{-i})$ and $(d';\mathbf Z_{-i})$ lying in $\mathcal Z$ with probability one and the expectations being finite. Let $\hat\tau_N$ be an estimator, $s_N>0$ a deterministic sequence (the estimator's standard-error scale) and $\hat s_N$ an estimator of it. Suppose first-order inference on the AEED is valid: $(\hat\tau_N-T_N)/s_N$ converges in distribution to a law $L$ (the standard normal law when a central limit theorem holds) and $\hat s_N/s_N\to1$ in probability. If in addition $$|T_N-A_N|=o(s_N),$$ then $(\hat\tau_N-A_N)/\hat s_N$ converges in distribution to $L$. For every fixed $q>0$ such that $L(\{-q\})=L(\{q\})=0$, the intervals $\hat\tau_N\pm q\,\hat s_N$ have the same limiting coverage $L([-q,q])$ for the average direct effect and for the AEED; explicitly, $$\Pr\bigl[|\hat\tau_N-B_N|\le q\,\hat s_N\bigr]\longrightarrow L([-q,q])\qquad\text{for each }B_N\in\{T_N,A_N\}. $$ The endpoint condition is automatic when $L$ is continuous. The rate condition cannot be weakened to $|T_N-A_N|=o(1)$: under the same first-order AEED convergence and scale-consistency assumptions, if instead $(T_N-A_N)/s_N\to c\ne0$, then $(\hat\tau_N-A_N)/\hat s_N$ converges in distribution to the law of $L$ shifted by $c$, and P061-T4 gives a design with $T_N-A_N\to0$ and $|T_N-A_N|/s_N\to\infty$.
A sufficient condition for the rate condition. Suppose that at fixed own assignment $e\in\{d,d'\}$ unit $i$'s outcome is a function $f_{i,e}(\mathbf Z_{H_i})$ of the assignments of a set $H_i$ of other units, with range $R_{i,e}=\max f_{i,e}-\min f_{i,e}$; let $Q_{i,e}$ be the conditional law of $\mathbf Z_{H_i}$ given $Z_i=e$ and $Q_i$ its unconditional law. Then $$|T_N-A_N|\le L_N:=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\Big\{R_{i,d}\,\mathrm{TV}(Q_{i,d},Q_i)+R_{i,d'}\,\mathrm{TV}(Q_{i,d'},Q_i)\Big\},$$ so $L_N=o(s_N)$ suffices.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
$T_N$: the AEED of Equation (8), p. 7 (S6), for the $N$th population of the sequence of supplement p. 5 (S9). $y_i(d;\mathbf Z_{-i})$: footnote 8, p. 7, read as in (S10)(e). $s_N$, $\hat s_N$, $L$ and the phrase ‘first-order inference is valid’ are not objects of the paper, which says only ‘inference on AEEDs is asymptotically equivalent to inference on the “average direct effect”’; they are Sol's and the validator's formalization of that phrase for a common estimator and a common scale. The supplement's own description of valid inference (p. 6): “In settings where an appropriate CLT holds, the limiting variance is nondegenerate, and the variance estimator is consistent or conservative in a suitable asymptotic sense, Wald-type confidence intervals formed under a normal approximation have asymptotically valid, possibly conservative, coverage.” Total variation distance of two distributions on a finite set: $\mathrm{TV}(Q,P)=\tfrac12\sum_x|Q(x)-P(x)|$. $\mathbf Z_{H_i}$: the assignments of the units in $H_i$.
Domains and existence conditions: $N$ ranges over positive integers and $i=1,\ldots,N$; the fixed target labels $d,d'$ are real. The $N$th design is the paper's discrete design (S1, S2, S9): a probability mass function on the feasible assignment set $\mathcal Z_N\subseteq\mathbb R^N$, whose support $\{\mathbf z\in\mathcal Z_N:\Pr[\mathbf Z=\mathbf z]>0\}$ is countable but need not be finite (S10(a),(b)); expectations are absolutely convergent sums over the support. Outcomes are real functions $y_{i,N}:\mathcal Z_N\to\mathbb R$ and exposures are the coordinates $g_{i,N}(\mathbf z)=z_i$. For every $N,i$ and $e\in\{d,d'\}$, $\pi_{i,N}(e)=\Pr[Z_i=e]>0$ and $\mathrm E[|y_{i,N}(\mathbf Z)|\,\mathbb 1\{Z_i=e\}]<\infty$, so $T_N=N^{-1}\sum_i(\mathrm E[y_{i,N}(\mathbf Z)\mid Z_i=d]-\mathrm E[y_{i,N}(\mathbf Z)\mid Z_i=d'])$ exists. Both own-coordinate hybrids lie in $\mathcal Z_N$ for every assignment in the support (that is, almost surely) and, for every $N,i$, $\mathrm E|y_{i,N}(d;\mathbf Z_{-i})-y_{i,N}(d';\mathbf Z_{-i})|<\infty$. Separate integrability of the two hybrid responses is not required by the transfer result. The estimator and estimated scale are real functions of the $N$th assignment. In a studentized statistic, set the quotient to zero on $\{\hat s_N=0\}$ (any real convention there gives the same limit). Scale consistency and $s_N>0$ imply $\Pr[\hat s_N\le0]\to0$, so no everywhere-positive estimated-scale assumption is needed. Coverage is the displayed event $|\hat\tau_N-B_N|\le q\hat s_N$; on $\{\hat s_N>0\}$ it is exactly membership in the closed interval with the displayed endpoints. $L$ is any Borel probability law on $\mathbb R$; the coverage conclusion is restricted to fixed positive half-widths whose two endpoints have zero $L$-mass.
In the local bound, $H_i\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\{i\}$, and for every $N,i$ and $e\in\{d,d'\}$, $y_{i,N}(e;\mathbf Z_{-i})=f_{i,e}(\mathbf Z_{H_i})$ almost surely under the unconditional $N$th design. $\mathbf Z_{H_i}$ takes only finitely many values with positive probability, so $Q_i$, and $Q_{i,d}$ and $Q_{i,d'}$ (absolutely continuous with respect to $Q_i$ because $\pi_{i,N}(e)>0$), are distributions on a finite set, to which the total-variation formula above applies; finite support of the whole assignment design, a common finite assignment alphabet, or a full product feasible set is not required. Each $f_{i,e}$ is defined on a set of neighborhood configurations containing every value taken by $\mathbf Z_{H_i}$ with positive probability, and the displayed maximum and minimum over that set exist (for instance, when that set is the finite set of such values). All quantities with a unit index may also depend on $N$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (L1) For each $N$, since both targets are deterministic: $\dfrac{\hat\tau_N-A_N}{s_N}-\dfrac{\hat\tau_N-T_N}{s_N}=\dfrac{T_N-A_N}{s_N}$ (derivation.md, equation (1)). (L2) For distributions $Q,P$ on a finite set and a function $f$ with range $R$: $|\mathrm E_Qf-\mathrm E_Pf|\le R\,\mathrm{TV}(Q,P)$ (equation (13)). (L3) The bound $|T_N-A_N|\le L_N$ displayed in the statement (equation (14)). (L4) If the individual assignments are mutually independent, $Q_{i,e}=Q_i$ and $T_N=A_N$ exactly (also P061-T3(i)). (L5) Under uniform complete randomization of $n$ of $N$ units ($1\le n\le N-1$) with binary assignments, $|H_i|\le k_N$ and $R_{i,e}\le R_N$: $\mathrm{TV}(Q_{i,1},Q_{i,0})\le\dfrac{k_N}{N-1}$ and $L_N\le\dfrac{R_Nk_N}{N-1}$. (L6) In the design of P061-T4, $R_{i,e}=a$ and $\mathrm{TV}(Q_{i,e},Q_i)=\rho/2$, so $L_N=a\rho=T_N-A_N$: the bound is attained.
canonical_claim.note: Sections 2 and 4 of the validator's derivation. Sol's repair reads: for individualistic assignment mappings, valid first-order AEED inference transfers to the displayed direct effect provided $|\tau_{\mathrm{AEED}}-\tau_{\mathrm{direct}}|=o(s_N)$, where $s_N$ is the estimator's inferential scale; assumptions implying this condition must be specified. The repair cost is a new assumption that applications may not satisfy. The step from (L1) to the conclusion is Slutsky's theorem, which is the asymptotic part of the target; (L1)–(L6) are exact for each $N$. The settled record adds a sufficient condition from the cited literature (Sävje, Aronow and Hudgens, arXiv v4, Supplement A, Lemma A20: $|\tau_{\mathrm{adse}}-\tau_{\mathrm{eate}}|\le6k^2n^{-1}\alpha_{\mathrm{int}}$, so $\alpha_{\mathrm{int}}=o(Ns_N)$ suffices alongside valid AEED inference); it is not part of this target because that work is not staged and its quantities are not defined in the paper. The sufficient conditions (L3)–(L5) are derived by the validator and are not represented as conditions of Sävje (2024). The statement concerns a common estimator and scale; it does not assert that two independently chosen inference procedures agree.
